newsitem.title: UK: Britain could dominate Euro pensions market - report.
newsitem.headline: Britain could dominate Euro pensions market - report.

text.p: British pension fund managers could dominate a vast, potentially lucrative market in Europe but the UK must fully engage in monetary union to take advantage of the opportunity, a report from a European think-tank said.

The London-based Action Centre for Europe (ACE), whose president is former Conservative Party Chancellor Geoffrey Howe, said in a report released on Wednesday that the British financial services industry was well placed to "penetrate the fast-growing private pensions markets of continental Europe".

"Realistically, however, this opportunity is only fully available ...if the UK becomes part of the single currency. If Britain opts out, continental investment in UK securities would be outside currency-matching requirements."

The report slammed "glaring mistakes" in a recent British parliamentary report on pensions in Europe, adding that media coverage of it produced "irresponsible scare stories about European pensions (which are) no more convincing than other Euro-myths such as the straight banana and the square strawberry".
But there was undoubtedly a push for private pension provision, offering a large market, it added.

"If 60 percent of all potential EU participants are to be covered by funded pensions and if they are provided with a pension equivalent to 25 percent of previous earnings, the combines European pension fund asset base would expand ninefold to 10.2 trillion Ecu by 2020," the report said.
"This would represent a vast market, twice the size of the current American pension funds market."

The UK, which currently has more pension fund assets than the rest of the EU put together (80 percent of which is invested in equities), has the "size, expertise and experience to further increase its business".
The Centre also urged Britain to get behind the European Commission's effort to liberalise pensions marketing in Europe, as freedom to invest is enshrined in the Maastricht Treaty.
A 1994 European-wide Pensions Directive was supported by the UK but failed after four years of talks "partly because of Britain's perceived hostility to European integration".

The ACE report said progress towards monetary union and the single currency "will by definition eliminate the currency matching restrictions on investment that currently exist in some EU member states".
"Britain would do well to stress its pro-European stance on pensions reform rather than to use future pensions liabilities as another excuse for non-participation in a single currency."
